objectives: Map global health governance (WHO, GFATM, Gavi, IHR).
Explain why pandemic preparedness is a coordination problem.
Reason about One Health + zoonotic spillover risks.

slides.title: The architecture of global health
slides.body:
**Global health** = health beyond national boundaries, recognizing interdependence + shared determinants. Modern architecture (multilateral, public-private, civil-society):

• **WHO** (World Health Organization, 1948): UN specialized agency; sets norms, supports member states, runs disease-control programs, manages IHR. Funded ~20% by assessed contributions, 80% voluntary donations.
• **Global Fund (GFATM)**: financing for HIV, TB, malaria. ~$5B/yr. Performance-based grants to countries.
• **Gavi, the Vaccine Alliance**: bulk-procures childhood vaccines for low-income countries; immunized 1B+ children since 2000.
• **PEPFAR** (US, 2003): largest HIV bilateral; helped scale ART globally.
• **Unitaid, FIND, MPP, etc.**: market-shaping for diagnostics + drugs.
• **GPEI** (Global Polio Eradication Initiative): >99% reduction in polio since 1988; close to eradication.
• **Civil society + NGOs**: MSF, Partners In Health, BRAC, etc.

**International Health Regulations (IHR, revised 2005)**: legally binding framework for 196 countries. Requires reporting of 'events of international concern' (PHEIC); WHO can issue temporary recommendations.

PHEICs declared: H1N1 2009, polio 2014, Ebola 2014, Zika 2016, Ebola 2019, COVID-19 2020 (declared Jan 30, 2020), mpox 2022, mpox 2024. Each tested + revealed gaps in the system.

slides.title: Why pandemic preparedness is hard
slides.body:
Pandemics + global health threats share structural challenges:

• **Externalities + free-riding**: every country wants others to invest in preparedness while underinvesting itself. Surveillance, vaccine R&D, stockpiling are public goods with under-provision absent coordination.
• **Sovereignty tensions**: IHR requires reporting + cooperation but lacks enforcement; countries fear travel/trade restrictions + may delay reporting (early COVID-19, MERS).
• **Time inconsistency**: post-crisis attention spikes (SARS 2003, H1N1 2009, Ebola 2014, COVID-19 2020); preparedness funding cycles + then declines as memory fades.
• **Wealth disparities**: rich countries access vaccines / drugs / treatments first; low-income countries last (vaccine equity in COVID-19 was a major moral + epidemiological failure).
• **Misinformation**: pandemic-era trust deficits undermine compliance, vaccination, accurate reporting.
• **Surveillance gaps**: most spillovers occur in resource-poor settings with limited laboratory + epidemiological capacity.
• **'Spilled milk' problem**: investments that *prevent* a pandemic look wasteful if the pandemic doesn't happen; political economy favors response over prevention.

COVID-19 exposed all these. Post-COVID response: WHO Pandemic Agreement negotiations (2024-25, status uncertain); proposed Independent Panel for Pandemic Preparedness + Response (IPPPR); CEPI 100-day mission for new vaccines; Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations; ACT-A (Access to COVID-19 Tools).

The central preparedness question: can the international system coordinate effectively when individual incentives push against cooperation? An open question that the next pandemic will test.

slides.title: One Health + zoonotic spillover
slides.body:
**One Health**: human, animal, + environmental health are interconnected. Most emerging infectious diseases are **zoonotic** — originated in animals + jumped to humans.

**Recent zoonotic spillovers**:
• HIV (chimp/bonobo → human, ~1908, central Africa).
• Ebola (fruit bat reservoir, multiple human outbreaks).
• MERS-CoV (camel → human, ~2012).
• SARS-CoV-1 (civet → human, 2002-03).
• SARS-CoV-2 (likely bat → intermediate → human, 2019; ongoing debate).
• Nipah, Hendra (bat → human/livestock).
• Influenza pandemic strains (avian + swine → human; 1918, 1957, 1968, 2009).
• Mpox (rodent reservoir; 2022 outbreak in non-endemic countries).

Drivers of spillover (Jones+ 2008 Nature; Plowright+ 2017):
1. **Wildlife-human contact**: deforestation, bushmeat hunting, wet markets, urban encroachment.
2. **Agricultural intensification**: factory farming with stressed animals + dense populations (avian flu).
3. **Climate change**: shifting animal ranges + behavior.
4. **Travel + trade**: rapid global spread once jump occurs.
5. **Antimicrobial use** in livestock: drives resistance.

**Prevention strategies**: surveillance of wildlife + livestock; sentinel veterinary monitoring; deforestation + biodiversity protection; safer wildlife trade regulation; antimicrobial stewardship; better PPE + risk-communication for animal workers; rapid genome-sequencing capacity.

**Investments**: PREDICT project (USAID, ended 2020 + partially restored as DEEP VZN); Global Virome Project; EcoHealth Alliance; WHO+FAO+WOAH (animal health) tripartite. Debate over how broadly to surveil + how much to fund — high-risk-high-reward science with diffuse public benefit.

question.question: Reason through vaccine equity during the COVID-19 pandemic
question.goal: By December 2021, wealthy countries had administered ~70% of available COVID-19 vaccine doses; some countries in sub-Saharan Africa had <5% coverage. Walk through what went wrong + what could improve next time.

steps.prompt: What was the proposed mechanism for equitable distribution?
hints: A global multilateral procurement + distribution mechanism.
steps.reveal: COVAX: ACT-Accelerator's vaccine pillar; co-led by Gavi + CEPI + WHO. Aimed to procure + distribute 2B doses to 92 lower-income countries by end of 2021, with self-financing for higher-income countries.

hints: Wealthy countries acted directly with manufacturers.
steps.reveal: (1) **Bilateral deals + advance-purchase agreements** by wealthy countries (US, EU, UK) secured early supply before COVAX could place orders. (2) **Manufacturing concentration**: most mRNA production in US/EU; India's Serum Institute (key COVAX supplier) faced export ban after Delta wave. (3) **IP barriers**: vaccine patents + technology-transfer concerns limited diversification. (4) **Cold-chain + delivery capacity gaps** in recipient countries.

steps.prompt: What was the consequence — for both ethics + global pandemic dynamics?
steps.motivation: Variant emergence, prolonged pandemic, moral failures.
hints: What happens when transmission remains high?
steps.reveal:
(1) **Variant emergence**: Omicron likely emerged in unvaccinated populations with high transmission (South Africa) — eventually spread globally + reinfected vaccinated populations. (2) **Prolonged pandemic**: low coverage = ongoing transmission = ongoing healthcare strain + deaths in low-income settings. (3) **Moral failures**: WHO Director-General Tedros called it a 'moral catastrophe' — preventable deaths in low-income countries.

Vaccine equity is also self-interest: ongoing global transmission breeds variants that affect everyone.

(1) **Distributed manufacturing**: mRNA tech-transfer hubs (WHO South Africa hub launched 2022 — making Moderna analog without licensing). (2) **Pre-arranged financing** + binding multilateral commitments (WHO Pandemic Agreement, in negotiation). (3) **Pre-positioned regulatory pathways** + WHO emergency-use listings to accelerate approvals. (4) **R&D commitments** with equitable-access conditions (CEPI 100-day mission). (5) **Stockpiling regional + diversified**. (6) **Capacity-building** in recipient countries: regulatory, cold-chain, delivery, training. (7) **Trade flexibilities**: TRIPS waivers, technology-transfer requirements built into emergency declarations.

The WHO Pandemic Agreement (final text 2024-25) attempts many of these — but binding force + buy-in remain contested.

question.question: Why is malaria still endemic in sub-Saharan Africa despite >50 years of intensified control, while it was eliminated from much of the temperate world?
options: Multiple structural drivers: (1) Anopheles mosquito species in Africa (esp. An. gambiae) are highly anthropophilic + efficient vectors; (2) Year-round transmission climate; (3) Poverty + weak health systems; (4) Drug + insecticide resistance; (5) P. falciparum (more deadly + complex) dominates vs P. vivax / malariae elsewhere; (6) Vaccine development was historically underfunded relative to disease burden. Most non-African elimination relied on temperate climate breaking transmission seasonally + economic development enabling housing + sanitation improvements.
Malaria is genetic and only affects certain populations.
Malaria has been eliminated everywhere except where conspiracy theories prevent control.
question.explanation:
Malaria control history:

• **WHO Global Malaria Eradication Programme (1955-1969)**: DDT spraying + chloroquine. Eliminated malaria from Europe, Caribbean, parts of US, Singapore, much of Asia. Failed in Africa: too efficient vectors + insufficient infrastructure.
• Effort abandoned (1969); replaced with control focus.
• **Roll Back Malaria (1998-)**: ITNs (insecticide-treated nets), IRS (indoor residual spraying), ACTs (artemisinin combination therapies), case management.
• Deaths dropped from ~860K (2000) to ~600K (2022) globally. ~96% of malaria deaths in sub-Saharan Africa.
• Recent setbacks: insecticide resistance, ACT resistance in Southeast Asia (artemisinin failure in Cambodia spreading to Africa).

Structural reasons for African persistence:
1. **An. gambiae complex**: highly anthropophilic (prefers humans), endophilic (rests in houses), long-lived, abundant. An. gambiae s.s. is among the most efficient malaria vectors known.
2. **Climate**: year-round warm + humid; vector abundant + transmission continuous.
3. **P. falciparum dominance**: most deadly Plasmodium species; complex life cycle resists drug + immune control.
4. **Health system + poverty**: limited diagnosis, drug access, vector control.
5. **Drug + insecticide resistance**: chloroquine (1970s-90s); pyrethroid (2010s+); artemisinin (Southeast Asia, spreading).

Progress: **RTS,S (Mosquirix) vaccine** approved 2021 for African children; **R21/Matrix-M** approved 2023 with higher efficacy. Both have ~70-77% reduction in severe malaria episodes. First malaria vaccines approved after >30 yr development. Coupled with bednets + ACTs + monoclonals, control is finally improving — but elimination requires sustained, integrated effort + new tools.

hints: What's special about the African Anopheles?
slides.workedSolution: African An. gambiae is hyper-anthropophilic + abundant + long-lived + bites humans efficiently. Climate year-round warm + humid. P. falciparum dominates (most deadly + complex). Poverty + weak health systems. Insecticide + drug resistance emerged. Non-African elimination relied on temperate climate breaking transmission + economic development. Africa needs sustained ITNs + IRS + ACTs + new vaccines (RTS,S 2021, R21 2023) + monoclonals. Progress slow but accelerating.

question.question: What's the strongest argument for 'One Health' surveillance as pandemic preparation?
options: ~75% of emerging infectious diseases are zoonotic; spillover is the upstream event of pandemics; integrated surveillance of wildlife, livestock, + humans can detect novel pathogen emergence before human-to-human spread becomes established. Cost: a fraction of pandemic response. Examples: H5N1 surveillance pre-empted 2009 H1N1 mitigation; SARS-CoV-1 traced to civets enabled mid-2003 containment; Nipah surveillance in Bangladesh enables outbreak control.
It's required by law in all countries.
Surveillance is always cheap and easy.
question.explanation:
**Zoonotic emergence + spillover** is the entry point for most pandemics:
• HIV: ~1908 spillover, decades to recognition.
• SARS-CoV-1: civet/bat → human Nov 2002.
• SARS-CoV-2: bat → intermediate? → human late 2019.
• H5N1, H7N9: avian flus, repeated near-misses.
• Ebola: bat reservoir, multiple human outbreaks.
• Nipah: bat → pig/human, recurring outbreaks.
• Mpox: rodent reservoir → human + intra-human chains since 2022.

**Integrated surveillance** (One Health) detects emergence at the human-animal-environment interface:
- Wildlife sampling (e.g., PREDICT identified ~1000 viruses, some now-known pandemic threats).
- Livestock surveillance (avian influenza in poultry).
- Animal worker sentinels (vets, abattoir workers).
- Wastewater + environmental sampling.
- Rapid genomic sequencing.

**Cost-effectiveness**:
- Pandemic response cost (COVID-19): >$10T globally.
- Preparedness + surveillance: ~$5-10B/yr globally (proposed).
- Even if surveillance reduces pandemic likelihood by 10%, the math is overwhelmingly favorable.

**Limits**:
- Sampling space is vast (>1.7M unknown viruses in mammals + birds; ~600K-800K with zoonotic potential).
- Few will spill over.
- Risk of laboratory accident + gain-of-function research raises ethical questions.
- Political constraint + disease-stigma concerns can hamper international cooperation.

**Current investments**: WHO, FAO, WOAH (animal health) tripartite + UNEP form the Quadripartite. DEEP VZN, Global Virome Project, regional centers. Underfunded relative to pandemic risk; debate over targeting + intensity.

hints: What % of emerging diseases are zoonotic?
slides.workedSolution: ~75% of emerging infectious diseases are zoonotic. Spillover is upstream of pandemics. Integrated surveillance (wildlife + livestock + human + environment) detects emergence before sustained human-to-human spread. Cost: $5-10B/yr globally vs pandemic costs >$10T. Even small risk-reduction yields favorable cost-benefit. Limits: vast sampling space, biosafety/lab-accident risks, political coordination. Current programs: PREDICT/DEEP VZN, Global Virome Project, WHO+FAO+WOAH+UNEP Quadripartite. Underfunded relative to risk.

question.question: An estimated 75% of emerging infectious diseases originate in wildlife. If there are roughly 1.7 million unknown mammal + bird viruses + about half could potentially infect humans, approximately how many zoonotic threats are there in mammals + birds (in millions, to one decimal)?

question.prompt: In ≤120 words, explain to a national-government policy-maker why investing in pandemic preparedness is a 'no-brainer' economically but politically difficult to fund.
question.rubric: Mentions: pandemic costs (COVID-19 globally >$10T economic + ~7M+ excess deaths; future pandemics could be similar or worse). Preparedness costs (~$5-10B/yr globally) tiny in comparison; even a 1-10% risk reduction has very favorable cost-benefit. Components of preparedness: surveillance (incl. One Health), R&D (CEPI 100-day mission), manufacturing capacity, stockpiles, health-system capacity, governance + international coordination. Political difficulty: preparedness benefits are diffuse + delayed (and look 'wasted' if the pandemic doesn't happen); investments outside ministry of health + crowding out by other priorities; rich-poor country incentive mismatch (manufacturing in HICs but worst spillover risks in LMICs); attention fades after each crisis (cycle of panic + neglect). Concludes: requires institutional commitment (pre-arranged + binding financing) + sustained advocacy + reframing as economic + security policy not just health policy.
